content:
Critics say that Muhammad (peace be upon him) was hostile to Jews as a people. They point to the Quran verses about apes and pigs, to a hadith (a report of the Prophet's words or acts) that speaks of killing Jews, and to the Quran's remarks on Jewish groups.

Below are six points. Each objection is stated at full strength, the texts are quoted as they stand, and then each is read in its context and as the classical scholars read it. Some of the texts are hard, and none of them is softened here.

Three verses speak of a transformation. Quran 2:65 and 7:166 say of a group who broke the Sabbath: "Be apes, despised." Quran 7:163 sets the scene in a town by the sea whose people were tested over fishing on that day, and 2:66 calls the event an example and a lesson for the God-fearing.[1]

Quran 5:60 speaks of those whom God cursed and with whom He was angry, and "made among them apes and swine." It follows a rebuke of some of the People of the Book who mocked the Muslim call to prayer.[2]

The language is harsh, and a critic is right to say so. Read in sequence, though, all three verses describe a punishment that fell on identified wrongdoers in the past. The phrase "among them" in 5:60 marks a part of a community. No verse applies the words to Jews of a later age.

The commentators did not agree on whether the transformation was physical. Al-Tabari reports on 2:65 that Mujahid took it as a change of hearts and a parable, so that the sinners kept their human form. He also reports the view, attributed to Ibn Abbas, that they were changed in body, and he prefers it himself, holding that the plain wording of the Quran requires it.[3]

The sources also record a limit on how far the event reaches. A report in Sahih Muslim has the Prophet saying that God does not give a people He has transformed any descendants.[4] On that report the transformed people left no line, so the verses give no ground for describing later Jews in those terms.

Both readings treat the verses as a warning drawn from the history of one group. The Quran says as much about the event itself, calling it a lesson for those who fear God.

The Quran does criticise Jewish groups, and the criticism is real. It charges some with killing prophets without right, with breaking the covenant and with distorting the scripture.[5] It quotes the saying "God's hand is tied" and the claim that Ezra is the son of God, and it rejects both.[6] The verse on Ezra goes on to criticise Christian belief about the Messiah in the same breath.

Each charge is attached to a deed, a statement or "a party of them" (2:75). The same passages draw lines. Quran 3:113 says "they are not all alike" and describes a community among the People of the Book who recite God's verses at night, and 3:115 promises that no good they do will be denied.[7] Quran 5:69 gives the assurance of no fear and no grief to Jews, Christians and Sabians who believe in God and the Last Day and do good. Quran 7:159 speaks of a community among the people of Moses who guide by the truth.

Some early commentators held that 2:62, which has the same wording as 5:69, was limited by 3:85; others read it as standing.[8] The Quran never judges Jews as one body.

The sentence "just issue orders to kill every Jew present in the country" is real. It stands in Sahih al-Bukhari, in the opening report of the collection, the account of Heraclius and Abu Sufyan.[9] The speakers are Heraclius's courtiers. They observe that only Jews practise circumcision and urge him to order the killing of Jews in his realm. A messenger then tells him that the Arabs also circumcise, and the plan is dropped. Muhammad is absent from the scene, and no Muslim speaks the line.

The closest report that does concern Muhammad is Abu Dawud 3002. It has him say, "If you gain victory over the men of the Jews, kill them," and ties the words to the killing of a Jewish merchant by a Muslim named Muhayyisa.[10] It comes from Ibn Ishaq through an unnamed client of Zayd ibn Thabit, and it is graded weak (daif). Ibn Ishaq's account sets it after the killing of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, in the fighting at Medina. For peaceful non-Muslims the Quran sets another rule: God does not forbid kindness and justice toward those who have not fought you over religion (60:8).[11]

Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim both record that the Hour will not come until the Muslims fight the Jews, and that a Jew will hide behind a stone or tree, which will call to the Muslim to kill him, except the gharqad tree.[12] A critic who quotes it has invented nothing. It has been cited in modern political texts, including the 1988 charter of Hamas, and that use is a reason to read it with care.[13]

The text carries several qualifications. It is a prediction placed among the signs of the Hour, and it gives no instruction to anyone now. It describes a war, with fighting on both sides. The Quran meanwhile tells Muslims to be just even toward a people they dislike (5:8) and allows kindness toward those who do not fight them (60:8).[11] The classical rules for Jews and Christians living under Muslim rule were built on the Quran and on the Prophet's treaties and practice, and this report is no basis for them.

On reaching Medina, Muhammad made a written agreement, preserved in Ibn Ishaq's biography, that joined the Muslims and the Jewish clans of the city as one community for the defence of the town. It states that the Jews have their religion and the Muslims theirs.[14]

The relationship later broke down, and the record says so. The Banu Qaynuqa and the Banu Nadir were expelled after what the sources describe as breaches of the agreement. The men of the Banu Qurayza were put to death after the Battle of the Trench, by the judgment of Sa'd ibn Muadh, whose ruling the tribe had agreed to accept.[15] That is the hardest event in the record. The questions it raises concern the process, the numbers, which the sources and modern historians dispute, and the law applied. It was a verdict on one tribe accused of treachery in wartime and carried no general rule about Jews.

Ordinary dealings are also recorded. When Muhammad died, his armour was pledged to a Jewish man in return for grain bought on credit.[16]

The bottom line

The Quran criticises named Jewish groups for specific acts. The apes and pigs verses describe a past punishment, which the classical commentators read in two ways, and neither reading names Jews of today. The wording quoted as "kill every Jew" is spoken by Byzantine courtiers. The closest report about Muhammad is graded weak, and the end-of-time report is a prediction without an instruction.

The Quran also praises upright Jews, and the Prophet's dealings with Jewish tribes include both agreement and conflict. A critic may fairly call some of these texts severe. The sources give no support to the claim that Islam commands hatred of Jews as a people.

Notes

  1. Quran 2:65-66; 7:163-166.
  2. Quran 5:57-60.
  3. Al-Tabari, commentary on Quran 2:65 (the views of Mujahid and Ibn Abbas).
  4. Sahih Muslim 2663b (Book of Destiny): "Allah did not cause the race of those which suffered metamorphosis to grow.". Checked on sunnah.com: the report of Abdullah ibn Masud on the request of Umm Habiba, with the remark that the transformed groups left no offspring.
  5. Quran 2:61; 2:75; 5:13.
  6. Quran 5:64; 9:30.
  7. Quran 3:113-115; 5:69; 7:159.
  8. Al-Tabari, commentary on Quran 2:62, with Quran 3:85: he records the report from Ibn Abbas that 3:85 came after 2:62, and the views of Mujahid and al-Suddi that the verse stands.
  9. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Beginning of Revelation, the report of Heraclius and Abu Sufyan (hadith 7 in the sunnah.com numbering).
  10. Sunan Abi Dawud 3002 (Book of Tribute, Spoils and Rulership), chapter "How were the Jews expelled from Medina?"; graded weak by al-Albani; Ibn Hisham, Sira, vol. 2, pp. 54–58, places the killing of Ibn Sunayna after the killing of Kab ibn al-Ashraf. Checked on sunnah.com: Sunan Abi Dawud 3002, report of Muhayyisa, graded da'if (weak) by al-Albani.
  11. Quran 60:8; Quran 5:8.
  12. Sahih al-Bukhari 2926 (Book of Jihad), the chapter on fighting the Jews; Sahih Muslim 2922 (Book of Tribulations and Portents of the Hour), with the gharqad tree. Checked on sunnah.com: Sahih Muslim 2922, report of Abu Hurayra (the gharqad tree). Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 6, p. 103 (Shamela text), for Bukhari 2926.
  13. Charter of the Islamic Resistance Movement (Hamas), 1988, article 7.
  14. Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, in the recension of Ibn Hisham, the document of Medina.
  15. Sahih al-Bukhari 4121 (Book of Military Expeditions), the Banu Qurayza and the judgment of Sa'd ibn Muadh; Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah. Checked on sunnah.com: Sahih al-Bukhari 4121, report of Abu Said al-Khudri on the judgment of Sad ibn Muadh over Banu Qurayza.
  16. Sahih al-Bukhari 2916 (Book of Jihad): he "died while his (iron) armor was mortgaged to a Jew for thirty Sas of barley"; compare 2068 (Book of Sales). Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 6, p. 99 (Shamela text), for Bukhari 2916.
